name: Burkina Faso
card_headline: Burkina Faso's junta dissolved every political party and is shutting the UN rights office while JNIM fights the army and Islamic State and 4.5 million need aid.
card_summary: Captain Ibrahim Traoré has ruled since September 2022, and elections were pushed to 2029. All political parties were dissolved on 29 January 2026. [1] JNIM, linked to al-Qaeda, mounted a large offensive in February and now also fights Islamic State's Sahel branch. [2][3] ACLED data show state forces killed more civilians than jihadists in 2025. [4] The UN counts 4.5 million people in need. [5] The army's claim to hold 74 percent of the territory is contested. [2]
card_local: Local sourcing is thin in this draft. Burkina24's report of the 5 November cabinet meeting says the Patriotic Support Fund raised 250.16 billion F CFA by 29 September, mostly spent on the VDP militias. [6]
card_international: AFP and Reuters report JNIM's February offensive and the army's claim to hold 74 percent of the territory, and Al Jazeera reports Islamic State fighting JNIM on the northern border. [2][7][3]
card_scholar: ACLED counts about 320 clashes between JNIM and Islamic State's Sahel branch, and International IDEA says national consultations backed a five-year extension of military rule with no electoral timetable. [3][8]
context_md: Captain Ibrahim Traoré took power in September 2022, eight months after an earlier coup ousted President Roch Marc Kaboré. [9] The junta first promised ECOWAS elections by 2024, then moved the date to 2029 after a national conference that several parties boycotted. [9] Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger left ECOWAS in January 2025 to form the Alliance of Sahel States. [9] The junta ended security cooperation with France and has deepened ties with Russia, China, Iran and Türkiye. [8] More than 2.1 million people were internally displaced by April 2026, according to OCHA. [10] The electoral commission was dissolved in July 2025, and all political parties followed on 29 January 2026. [9]

sections.title: JNIM is fighting the army and Islamic State at once, and the 74 percent claim is contested
sections.body_md:
The army said in mid-February that it controls 74 percent of the national territory and has retaken 600 villages. AFP notes that the army rarely comments on attacks. [2] Other estimates are lower. Al Jazeera cites the Africa Center for Strategic Studies as saying armed groups control about 60 percent of the country. [9] It also reports that the International Crisis Group places JNIM in extensive areas of the north, north-centre, west and east. [3] No source read for this draft reconciles these figures.

The state's own account comes through Sidwaya, which cites the state news agency AIB and unnamed security sources. It says the army retook Tongomayel, Béléhédé and Pobé-Mengao in February and neutralised more than a hundred attackers. None of this is independently confirmed. [11]

JNIM's February offensive shows the scale of the fighting. ACLED analyst Heni Nsaibia said over 130 people died in battles between 12 and 22 February, among them soldiers, civilian auxiliaries and JNIM fighters. About 50 forestry officers were killed in an ambush at Tandjari, and JNIM claims it killed dozens of soldiers at Titao, which is unverified. [2] Reuters, citing internal reports of two diplomatic missions, put the dead at more than 180 and reported nearly 80 soldiers and militia members killed at Titao. Burkina Faso's authorities did not respond to Reuters. [7] The monitoring group SITE told Reuters that JNIM claimed nearly 500 attacks in Burkina Faso in 2025. [7] ACLED's December review adds that JNIM ambushed a convoy near Koubel-Alpha in September 2025, killing about 90 soldiers, and briefly seized the provincial capitals Djibo and Diapaga in May 2025. [12]

Since early September 2026 JNIM has also been fighting Islamic State Sahel Province. Al Jazeera reports that ACLED counts about 320 clashes between the two groups and more than 2,200 fighter deaths since the rivalry began. The Islamic State affiliate claims over 200 JNIM fighters killed at Kacham, which nobody has verified. Nsaibia says the infighting is forcing JNIM to divert fighters from its war on governments. [3]

lenses.local: Burkina24's report of the 5 November cabinet meeting says the Patriotic Support Fund took in 87.77 billion F CFA in the third quarter, with most spending going to the VDP militias. [6]
lenses.international: AFP and Reuters report the February offensive, and Reuters says the authorities did not respond to its request for comment. [2][7]
lenses.scholar: ACLED's Nsaibia argues that the war with Islamic State is draining JNIM, and ACLED's December review says JNIM's sieges have weakened state control. [3][12]

sections.title: State forces and militias killed more civilians than the jihadists in 2025, ACLED data show
sections.body_md:
ACLED's data, carried by Reuters on 2 April 2026, show that in 2025 the Burkinabe military and its Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDP) killed 523 civilians, against 339 killed by JNIM and Islamic State Sahel Province. [4] Human Rights Watch reached a similar direction in a longer study. It documented at least 1,837 civilian killings in 57 incidents across 11 regions between January 2023 and August 2025. It attributes at least 1,255 deaths in 33 incidents to the army and VDP and at least 582 in 24 attacks to JNIM, with that split covering January 2023 to April 2025. [13]

HRW says all sides committed war crimes and that some acts amount to crimes against humanity. Its named cases include more than 400 civilians killed around Djibo in December 2023 by military and militia forces, and at least 133 killed by JNIM at Barsalogho on 24 August 2024. HRW says Traoré and six senior commanders may bear command responsibility, and that officials have denied or downplayed abuses. [14]

Attacks continued in 2026. HRW documented at least 38 civilians killed by JNIM in Titao and Manni in February, and says the state broadcaster reported army airstrikes and a BIR21 ground response at Titao. [15] On 1 September JNIM attacked an artisanal gold site at Soubo, in Yatenga, killing 24 civilians according to HRW's interviews, satellite imagery and a victim list. JNIM's Sharia Committee told HRW the dead were VDP members and "not civilians". Witnesses told HRW that no soldiers or VDP were present. HRW's page reports no government response. [16]

The two data sets use different methods and periods, so their totals cannot be added together. [4][13]

lenses.local: The state broadcaster's account of the Titao response reaches this draft only through HRW. [15]
lenses.international: Reuters and AFP carried the ACLED and HRW figures, and AFP reports no government reply. [4][13]
lenses.scholar: ACLED's conflict data and HRW's field research are the main independent sources on who kills civilians. [4][14]

sections.title: No political parties, no vote before 2029, and unconfirmed reports of a rift inside the junta
sections.body_md:
Traoré took power in September 2022 and the junta first promised ECOWAS elections by 2024. The government later moved the date to 2029 after a national conference that several parties boycotted. [9] International IDEA notes that those consultations backed a five-year extension with no electoral timetable and took place while parties were suspended. [8] The junta dissolved the Independent National Electoral Commission in July 2025, citing cost. [9]

On 29 January 2026 a decree adopted by the council of ministers dissolved all political parties and moved their assets to the state. Interior Minister Emile Zerbo said the step was part of an effort to rebuild the state and that the growth in parties had caused excesses. More than 100 parties were registered before the 2022 coup. [1] In April, on state television, Traoré said "la démocratie n'est pas faite pour nous", meaning democracy is not for Burkina Faso. [17]

Authorities announced in early January that they had foiled a plot to kill Traoré. Security Minister Mahamadou Sana announced it on television, and AP's report names no suspects. [18] A BBC report republished by Eye Radio says the government accused the exiled former leader Paul-Henri Damiba of planning the attack and said Ivory Coast funded it with 70 million CFA francs. These are the government's allegations, and no denial was reported at the time. [19]

In July, Vanguard reported that Traoré told community leaders in Ouahigouya he would punish anyone who failed him, amid rumours of a power struggle. It says the intelligence chief Oumarou Yabre had not been seen publicly since late May, and that security officials alleged the junta spokesman Farouk Azaria Sorgho had been abducted by Traoré associates. The report rests on unnamed security sources, and this draft found no confirmation. [20]

On 28 September, four years into his rule, AP reported that Traoré presents himself as Sankara's heir and has moved away from France toward Russia. [21]

lenses.local: Togonews in Lomé carried Traoré's remarks from state television, and Burkina24 carries the government's own record of cabinet decisions. [17][6]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports the party ban, and AP says journalists, magistrates and civil society figures have been forcibly recruited and sent to the front. [1][21]
lenses.scholar: International IDEA's Koné and Zahar describe a transition with no timetable and an amended charter that strengthens executive powers. [8]

sections.title: Journalists conscripted, hundreds of associations shut within weeks, and the UN rights office told to leave
sections.body_md:
Amnesty says Burkina Faso's authorities forcibly disappeared the investigative journalist Atiana Serge Oulon, director of L'Événement, on 24 June 2024. It says the authorities use a 2023 emergency law to conscript critics, including journalists, into the army. The government later confirmed that Oulon and other journalists had been conscripted. Amnesty adds that L'Événement was suspended days before his abduction, and it cites an RSF investigation from May 2026 alleging that he was tortured in unofficial detention sites. [22] Amnesty also reports that Moussa Sareba of Fil Infos disappeared in August 2025 and remains missing. [22] RSF ranks Burkina Faso 110th of 180 countries for press freedom. [23]

Some conscripted people have come back. HRW reported in July 2025 that the authorities released journalists including Guezouma Sanogo, Boukari Ouoba and Luc Pagbelguem, and it urged the government to stop using conscription against the media. [24]

The state has also moved against associations. AFP reported on 13 May that 247 more had been suspended, bringing the count since mid-April to 811 suspended and 118 dissolved. The stated reason was non-renewal of governing bodies. [25] CIVICUS counts more than 1,000 suspended and rates civic space as repressed. It adds that the General Union of Burkina Students and the broadcaster TV5 Monde were suspended in May. [26] ACAPS counts 118 NGOs dissolved and more than 350 suspended in April. [27] The counts differ, and none comes from a government register read for this draft.

In February the government suspended the UN human rights office, weeks after Volker Türk urged it to halt the closing of civic space and drop the party ban. The office announced on 30 June that it would close. Foreign Minister Karamoko Jean Marie Traoré told the UN resident coordinator that international organisations act as a "super police". [28] HRW's World Report adds that Burkina Faso announced its withdrawal from the International Criminal Court in September 2025 and criminalised same-sex relations. [29]

lenses.local: Independent Burkinabe outlets were not read for this section. Amnesty reports that L'Événement was suspended days before its director was abducted. [22]
lenses.international: AFP carried the association suspensions, and AP says journalists and magistrates have been sent to the front. [25][21]
lenses.scholar: CIVICUS rates civic space as repressed, and RSF and Amnesty document conscription and unofficial detention. [26][23][22]

sections.title: 4.5 million need aid, the displacement count is three years old, and the army is accused of blocking exits
sections.body_md:
The UN's 2026 plan counts 4.5 million people in need and targets 2.7 million, with US$658.5 million required. It says humanitarian access is severely limited, and the hardest areas are reachable only by air or escorted convoy. [5] The displacement figure needs a caveat. OCHA reported more than 2.1 million internally displaced people in April 2026, but ACAPS and Al Jazeera say the latest consolidated official estimate dates to March 2023. [10][27][3] The government body CONASUR reports that more than 1 million people had returned home by July 2025, a figure the UN plan relays. [5] ACAPS records 11,316 people newly displaced in August 2026 and says armed groups have blockaded Djibo since February 2022. [27]

On food, FEWS NET's February outlook projects that Karo-Péli province will reach IPC Phase 4, emergency, between June and September 2026 without food assistance. It says supplies to blockaded municipalities depend on military escorts or air transport. [30] ACAPS projects 1.66 million people in Phase 3 or worse during the June to August lean season, 223,000 of them in Phase 4. [27] FEWS NET reports 386,157 newly displaced people registered in 2025 and 9,099 children under five admitted for acute malnutrition in the first six weeks of 2026. [30] UNHCR's operation was 20 percent funded in the first quarter, with US$20.35 million available against a US$100.4 million requirement. [31]

The New Humanitarian reported in July that soldiers and VDP block civilians from leaving besieged towns including Djibo and Kantchari. Its sources are civilians and aid workers who asked for anonymity. The government did not respond to its request for comment, and the outlet could not establish how many people have been stopped. It adds that the government says it has recaptured territory and enabled returns, and describes those claims as disputed. [32]

lenses.local: No Burkinabe outlet was read for this section, and the CONASUR return figure reaches this draft only through the UN plan. [5]
lenses.international: The New Humanitarian's anonymous sources describe army restrictions on leaving besieged towns, and the government gave no response. [32]
lenses.scholar: ACAPS and FEWS NET supply the technical projections of hunger and displacement. [27][30]

sections.title: Gold is the state's project: nationalised mines, a refinery and an underground shutdown at Mana
sections.body_md:
The World Bank says the economy grew an estimated 5.3 percent in 2025, up from 4.8 percent in 2024, with inflation at minus 0.5 percent, a deficit of 1.8 percent of GDP and extreme poverty down 5 percentage points. [33] The IMF's February review gives a different set: 5.0 percent growth for 2025, a deficit of 4.0 percent and public debt of 57.2 percent of GDP. Its summary and table label the growth years inconsistently, so those numbers need caution. The IMF disbursed about US$33.2 million under its Extended Credit Facility, approved a new US$124.3 million arrangement, and says security remains a material constraint. [34]

Gold is the main lever of state policy. Prime Minister Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo said the state mining company SOPAMIB had taken control of two industrial mines, Boungou and Wahgnion, formerly held by Endeavour Mining. That article dates from 2025 and says Burkina Faso produced over 57 tons of gold in 2023. [35] In late September 2026 Traoré inaugurated the country's first gold refinery, saying the state wants "the entire value chain in the country". [36] On 5 November the council of ministers created a state company, FASO SANU, to curb illegal artisanal gold mining and secure contested sites. SONASP will hold 50 percent of it and the Treasury 50 percent. [37][6]

Operating risk sits with the miners. Endeavour said underground mining at its Mana mine was suspended on 28 October after part of an access ramp subsided, and it does not expect underground work to resume before the second quarter of 2027. The company says the group remains on track for its full-year targets. [38] HRW says artisanal sites are a major JNIM revenue source, and that the government suspended artisanal mining in Ouahigouya district from 1 July to 30 September, a ban residents said was not enforced. [16]

The state funds the war through the Patriotic Support Fund. It collected 250.16 billion F CFA between 1 January and 29 September 2026, 125.08 percent of its annual target, with most spending going to the VDP. [6] Sidwaya, a former state paper, reported that collections by 28 June were up 66.73 percent on the same period of 2025. [39]

lenses.local: Burkina24 and Sidwaya report the Patriotic Support Fund totals from government statements, and Sidwaya is a former state paper. [6][39]
lenses.international: Semafor and Miningmx cover the refinery and the Mana shutdown. [36][38]
lenses.scholar: The World Bank and IMF report growth near 5 percent and name security as a constraint, though they differ on the 2025 deficit. [33][34]

sections.title: Russia, the Sahel alliance and a spillover that reaches Benin and Ghana
sections.body_md:
Burkina Faso left ECOWAS in January 2025 with Mali and Niger and formed the Alliance of Sahel States. International IDEA says it ended security cooperation with France and left the G5 Sahel. [9][8] ACLED reported on 20 April that the alliance had announced 15,000 troops for a joint Unified Force. [40]

Russia is the closest security partner. Reuters reported on 9 July that after talks in Niamey a joint statement welcomed growing military cooperation, and Moscow said it would keep helping strengthen the armed forces of the three states. The statement said, without evidence, that external state actors including Ukraine and France were involved in regional attacks. Both denied it. [41] In January, Russian state media reported talks with Burkina Faso's prime minister on a Russian telecommunications satellite for the alliance. Daba Finance says its scale and financing are unclear. [42]

The war also spills toward the coast. ACLED reports a regionwide JNIM offensive since early February that reached Benin, which recorded its deadliest year to date. [40] Viraj Pattni of the security firm Castor Vali warns that JNIM's expansion could raise the threat to Gulf of Guinea states. [3] Ghana's foreign ministry confirmed that eight tomato traders were among the dead at Titao, while AFP and HRW cite seven Ghanaians. [7][2][15] Crisis Group published an analysis in February titled Understanding JNIM's Expansion Beyond the Sahel. This draft read only its catalogue entry. [43]

lenses.local: Daba Finance, an Abidjan outlet, reports the satellite talks from Russian state media and quotes no Burkinabe official. [42]
lenses.international: Reuters carried the Russia joint statement, and Al Jazeera carried the Gulf of Guinea warning. [41][3]
lenses.scholar: International IDEA describes the sovereigntist turn as selective repositioning rather than withdrawal from engagement. [8]

sections.title: Fake Traoré videos reached millions, and an online militia targets journalists
sections.body_md:
Much of what circulates online about Burkina Faso's leader is false. Full Fact rated a video of Traoré giving a long speech on Western media as altered, and experts told it the footage is likely an AI deepfake. The page metadata showed 13 million views, and the earliest version Full Fact found came from a YouTube upload whose description calls it entirely fictional. [44] TheCable's fact-check desk traced pro-Traoré accounts posting false or AI-made content in May 2025. A video claiming Traoré had made the country tax-free used a manipulated clip of an August 2024 speech that did not mention taxes, and crowd footage presented as a rally for him came from a protest in Belgrade. TheCable reports that one researcher linked such narratives to a Russian troll factory, a view it attributes to the researcher and does not verify. [45]

The same online ecosystem is aimed at critics. RSF's July investigation describes BIR-C as an online militia linked to the junta that combines propaganda with harassment. RSF says the Sky News reporter Yousra Elbagir was targeted after an April documentary, with one member posting 26 times in 12 days using doctored images. It says smear campaigns preceded the conscription of two journalists, Yacouba Ladji Bama and Guezouma Sanogo. RSF linked phone numbers in a leaked chat group to Defence Minister Célestin Simporé, who did not respond to its requests. Wangnin Zerbo, whom RSF names, confirmed he is a member and said the group has "no contact with the authorities". [46]

State media carries the government's version of events. State Media Monitor describes the broadcaster RTB as state-owned, with a director-general appointed by the council of ministers. It cites a 2024 analysis finding that over 80 percent of RTB's political coverage favoured the government's narrative. [47]

lenses.local: State Media Monitor's profile of RTB is the main read on state television's editorial line, and this draft did not read RTB or AIB directly. [47]
lenses.international: Full Fact in London and TheCable in Lagos traced the false clips with reverse image searches and metadata. [44][45]
lenses.scholar: RSF's investigation of BIR-C is the main research on the online campaign, and no peer-reviewed study of it was read. [46]

reporters.name: Mubarak Aliyu
reporters.bio: Bylined the 13 November 2026 Al Jazeera report on fighting between JNIM and Islamic State Sahel Province, datelined Ouagadougou.
reporters.why: The report sets out the rival groups' claims, ACLED's counts and analysts' views in one place.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Shola Lawal
reporters.bio: Bylined the 30 January 2026 Al Jazeera explainer on the ban on political parties and what comes next.
reporters.why: Gives the transition timeline from the 2022 coup to the party ban in one article, with an analyst's view.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Heni Nsaibia
reporters.bio: Author of ACLED's 11 December 2025 report on economic warfare and militant expansion, and quoted by AFP and Al Jazeera on JNIM's 2026 offensive and its war with Islamic State.
reporters.why: His counts of battles and fatalities are the most cited independent numbers on the conflict.
reporters.label: ACLED

reporters.name: Ilaria Allegrozzi
reporters.role: Senior Sahel researcher, Human Rights Watch
reporters.bio: Quoted as HRW's senior Sahel researcher in HRW's 4 November 2026 report on the JNIM attack at Soubo.
reporters.why: HRW's Burkina Faso findings on killings by both sides come from this research team.
reporters.label: Human Rights Watch

reporters.name: Atiana Serge Oulon
reporters.role: Investigative journalist and director of L'Événement
reporters.bio: Described by Amnesty as an investigative journalist who reported on corruption in the security forces; Amnesty and RSF say armed men abducted him in Ouagadougou on 24 June 2024.
reporters.why: His case is the clearest example of the risks Burkinabe journalists face; the government says he was conscripted.
reporters.label: Amnesty International

reporters.name: Fleur Birba and Mouniratou Ouedraogo
reporters.bio: Bylined the 1 July 2026 Sidwaya report on Patriotic Support Fund totals, distributed by allAfrica.
reporters.why: Their report is one of the few local accounts of how the war is funded, and it carries the government's view. Sidwaya is a former state paper.
reporters.label: Sidwaya via allAfrica

reporters.name: Charlotte Green
reporters.role: News and online journalist, Full Fact
reporters.bio: Bylined Full Fact's 25 June 2025 check of a viral video of Traoré, which experts judged likely to be an AI deepfake.
reporters.why: Shows how fabricated clips of Traoré spread to millions of viewers.
reporters.label: Full Fact

reporters.name: Ayodele Oluwafemi
reporters.bio: Bylined TheCable's 17 May 2025 investigation of pro-Traoré accounts spreading false and AI-generated content.
reporters.why: Traces specific false claims about Burkina Faso to their original footage.
reporters.label: TheCable

reporters.name: Fahiraman Rodrigue Koné and Marie-Joëlle Zahar
reporters.bio: Named as the authors of International IDEA's brief on engaging with Sahelian transitions.
reporters.why: Their brief covers the party ban, the open-ended transition and options for outside governments.
reporters.label: International IDEA

reporters.name: Ernest Harsch
reporters.role: Author on Burkina Faso and Thomas Sankara
reporters.bio: Author of Burkina Faso: A History of Power, Protest and Revolution (2017); the listing says he has researched and reported on the country for more than three decades.
reporters.why: Gives the history behind the 2014 uprising and the later transitions.

books.author: Ernest Harsch

podcasts.why: Why Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger left ECOWAS, and how the alliance builds legitimacy. Predates the 2026 party ban.

sources.title: Burkina Faso: Islamist armed group targets civilians

scores.coverage_basis: AFP and Reuters filed on the February offensive and on the HRW and ACLED findings on civilian deaths, but the wire flow is episodic and follows major attacks. [2][7][4] ACLED, HRW and ACAPS publish steadily, while local reporting is limited by state control of the national broadcaster and the conscription of journalists. [12][27][47][22]

severity.basis: ACLED's Nsaibia counted over 130 dead in ten days of the February offensive, and ACLED data show 523 civilians killed by state forces and 339 by jihadist groups in 2025. [2][4]
4.5 million people need aid and more than 2.1 million are displaced, and FEWS NET projects emergency conditions in Karo-Péli without food assistance. [5][10][30]
All parties were dissolved on 29 January 2026, the UN rights office is closing, and HRW says abuses by all sides include crimes against humanity. [1][28][14]
Growth was near 5 percent in 2025, inflation was minus 0.5 percent and public debt was 57.2 percent of GDP, with security a constraint on the outlook. [33][34]
The February offensive, the party ban, the UN office closure and the JNIM and Islamic State war all fall within the last ten months, while growth held near 5 percent. [2][1][28][3]

parts.basis: Russia pledged continued help to the alliance's armed forces and discussed a satellite project, and Burkina Faso has deepened ties with China, Iran and Türkiye. [41][42][8]
Burkina Faso produced over 57 tons of gold in 2023, and the state is taking over mines and has opened a refinery. [35][36]
JNIM's offensive reached Benin, Ghanaian traders died at Titao, and Castor Vali warns of a wider Gulf of Guinea threat. [40][7][3]
More than 2 million people are displaced, and nearly 51,000 Burkinabe refugees arrived in Mali's Koro area between April and September 2025. [10][27]
The country left ECOWAS, announced its withdrawal from the ICC and has forced out the UN rights office. [9][29][28]

summary: Burkina Faso matters beyond its borders through the spread of JNIM toward coastal states, its place in the Russia-backed Sahel alliance, and its break with regional and UN accountability bodies. [40][41][28]
gi.up: A JNIM seizure of a regional capital such as Fada N'Gourma, or a large new Russian deployment.
gi.down: Sustained loss of ground by JNIM to the army or to Islamic State, and restored cooperation with ECOWAS and the UN.

gaps: Local sourcing is thin: Burkina24 and Sidwaya report government decisions and the Sidwaya items relay the state news agency AIB. Independent Burkinabe outlets such as Lefaso.net articles, L'Observateur Paalga and Le Pays were not read, and RTB and AIB were not read directly.

Almost every casualty total rests on one party: JNIM and Islamic State battlefield claims, anonymous diplomatic reports (Reuters), unnamed security sources (Sidwaya via AIB), or HRW's remote interviews. None was independently verified.
The Crisis Group report on JNIM's expansion (20 February 2026) was read only through a catalogue entry; its findings on territorial control are cited second-hand through Al Jazeera.
The army's 74 percent and the ACSS figure of about 60 percent use different definitions, and the ACSS figure was read only through Al Jazeera.

The World Bank and IMF disagree on 2025 growth (5.3 versus 5.0 percent) and the deficit (1.8 versus 4.0 percent), and the IMF document labels its growth years inconsistently; the full reports were not opened.
The displacement figure of 2.1 million is the UN's; the last consolidated government estimate dates to March 2023, and the CONASUR return figure was read only through the UN plan.

The Vanguard report on the absence of two senior junta figures and the government's coup-plot allegations against Damiba and Ivory Coast rest on unnamed officials or the government itself, with no independent confirmation or reply from the accused.
The date of the Mining.com article on SOPAMIB is inferred (April 2025), and the Semafor refinery article gives neither capacity nor builder.

No podcast episode dated 2026 on Burkina Faso was verified; the two listed are older. The two documentaries are older or favour the alliance governments, and their streaming availability was not confirmed.
No reporter profile from a Burkinabe independent outlet could be verified; the local reporters listed are known only through one article byline or through rights-group reports.
Counts of suspended and dissolved associations differ across AFP, CIVICUS and ACAPS and were not reconciled against a government register.

change_reason: v2: long-form issue sections, private-sector coverage, podcasts, media, fact-checks
local_md:
Burkina24's report of the 5 November cabinet meeting says the Patriotic Support Fund took in 87.77 billion F CFA in the third quarter, with most spending going to the VDP militias. [6]

The state broadcaster's account of the Titao response reaches this draft only through HRW. [15]

Togonews in Lomé carried Traoré's remarks from state television, and Burkina24 carries the government's own record of cabinet decisions. [17][6]

Independent Burkinabe outlets were not read for this section. Amnesty reports that L'Événement was suspended days before its director was abducted. [22]

No Burkinabe outlet was read for this section, and the CONASUR return figure reaches this draft only through the UN plan. [5]

Burkina24 and Sidwaya report the Patriotic Support Fund totals from government statements, and Sidwaya is a former state paper. [6][39]

Daba Finance, an Abidjan outlet, reports the satellite talks from Russian state media and quotes no Burkinabe official. [42]

State Media Monitor's profile of RTB is the main read on state television's editorial line, and this draft did not read RTB or AIB directly. [47]
international_md:
AFP and Reuters report the February offensive, and Reuters says the authorities did not respond to its request for comment. [2][7]

Reuters and AFP carried the ACLED and HRW figures, and AFP reports no government reply. [4][13]

Al Jazeera reports the party ban, and AP says journalists, magistrates and civil society figures have been forcibly recruited and sent to the front. [1][21]

AFP carried the association suspensions, and AP says journalists and magistrates have been sent to the front. [25][21]

The New Humanitarian's anonymous sources describe army restrictions on leaving besieged towns, and the government gave no response. [32]

Semafor and Miningmx cover the refinery and the Mana shutdown. [36][38]

Reuters carried the Russia joint statement, and Al Jazeera carried the Gulf of Guinea warning. [41][3]

Full Fact in London and TheCable in Lagos traced the false clips with reverse image searches and metadata. [44][45]
scholar_md:
ACLED's Nsaibia argues that the war with Islamic State is draining JNIM, and ACLED's December review says JNIM's sieges have weakened state control. [3][12]

ACLED's conflict data and HRW's field research are the main independent sources on who kills civilians. [4][14]

International IDEA's Koné and Zahar describe a transition with no timetable and an amended charter that strengthens executive powers. [8]

CIVICUS rates civic space as repressed, and RSF and Amnesty document conscription and unofficial detention. [26][23][22]

ACAPS and FEWS NET supply the technical projections of hunger and displacement. [27][30]

The World Bank and IMF report growth near 5 percent and name security as a constraint, though they differ on the 2025 deficit. [33][34]

International IDEA describes the sovereigntist turn as selective repositioning rather than withdrawal from engagement. [8]

RSF's investigation of BIR-C is the main research on the online campaign, and no peer-reviewed study of it was read. [46]
